interview_metadata.name: Melissa Ingram
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Iowa and I have lived in Neola pretty much my whole life. I am eight, so my life story is not super long yet, but it feels big to me. When I was little, I liked blocks and stuffed animals, and then I started making up stories where the couch was a mountain or my LEGO town had a castle and a space station. I go to elementary school, and I like reading chapter books, art time, music, and when we do group projects because I can help make the story part. My family is my mom, my dad, my little brother Tyler, and me, and we go to school things, church things, soccer, and sometimes the county fair. A big thing for me was learning to play keyboard, because at first I thought my fingers were too slow, but now I can play little songs. I also started soccer with the Neola Tigers, and I like running even when practice is over. I want to be an astronaut, artist, or veterinarian when I grow up, and maybe I can be all three if I make space paintings and help space animals.

follow_ups.question: What is one of your earliest memories?
follow_ups.response: I remember being small and making a blanket fort in the living room with my mom. I put stuffed animals inside and said it was a castle where everyone had strawberry smoothies.

follow_ups.question: Who has helped shape who you are so far?
follow_ups.response: My mom helps me with school stuff and art supplies, my dad helps me build LEGO things that do not fall down, and my teacher lets me read my stories sometimes.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: I think my crossroads was when I could pick soccer or just come home after school. I was nervous because I did not know if I would kick the ball wrong or if the other kids would be faster. My friend Emma said she was doing it, and my dad said I could try one practice and stop if I hated it. At first I ran after the ball too much and got tired, but then I scored one tiny practice goal and everyone clapped. After that I wanted to keep going. Now I think of myself as someone who can try a thing even when I feel shy first.

follow_ups.question: What did you do right before the first practice?
follow_ups.response: I put on my shin guards wrong and my mom fixed them in the car. I kept asking if we were late even though we were early.

follow_ups.question: Who did you talk to afterward?
follow_ups.response: I told my dad the whole drive home, and then I showed Tyler how I kicked the ball, but he mostly tried to run away with it.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: I made a choice, but it was a little choice. I said I would try soccer one time, and then it got easier after I was already there.

follow_ups.question: What helped you say yes?
follow_ups.response: Knowing I did not have to be perfect helped. Also Emma being there helped a lot.

follow_ups.question: Would you make the same choice again?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because now I like running and being on a team.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: My parents and coach already helped. It also helps when teams let new kids learn slowly and do not yell at them.

follow_ups.question: What did your coach do that helped?
follow_ups.response: She showed us where to stand and said good job when we tried, even if the ball went sideways.

follow_ups.question: What would make trying new activities easier?
follow_ups.response: If a friend can come with me and someone explains the rules before we start.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children because I am eight. My mom, Sarah, is really important because she packs my lunch, helps me practice spelling words, and lets me help make smoothies if I stay careful with the blender. My dad, Mark, is important too because he works hard and also plays catch with me or checks if my LEGO bridge is strong. My little brother Tyler is five and he can be annoying when he touches my stickers, but he is also funny and makes car noises when we build roads. I have grandparents nearby enough that we see them for Sunday meals or birthdays. Family is mostly who drives me places, listens to my stories, and tells me to find my missing folder before school.

follow_ups.question: What do you do with your family on a normal evening?
follow_ups.response: We eat dinner, do homework or reading, and sometimes I build LEGO while Tyler plays cars. If it is nice out, we go outside before bath time.

follow_ups.question: Who do you go to when you feel upset?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom first, but if I am mad about building something, I ask my dad because he is patient with pieces.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: We have a dog named Daisy. She is not a person, but she feels like family because she sleeps near my bed sometimes.

follow_ups.question: What do you do with Daisy?
follow_ups.response: I help put food in her bowl and I throw her tennis ball in the yard.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone else live with you?
follow_ups.response: No, just Mom, Dad, Tyler, Daisy, and me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are important. Emma is my best school friend, and we play tag and make up stories where we are sisters in a magic forest. I also like Jayden because he is good at soccer and does not get mad if someone misses. My teacher, Mrs. Bell, is important because she says I have good ideas and reminds me to slow down when I write. I do not have a romantic partner because I am a kid.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Emma?
follow_ups.response: Almost every school day, and sometimes at soccer or birthday parties.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your friends usually choose to play?
follow_ups.response: Tag, pretend castles, drawing contests, or building little LEGO towns if we are inside.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: Neola is small, and there are fields and houses and roads where you can see far. I like that I know some people at school and church, and sometimes we see the same families at the store or the fair. Our yard has places where I can run, and there are trees I like to climb when a grown-up says it is okay. It is not like a big city with giant buildings. It feels quiet, except when trucks go by or when kids are playing outside.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend the most time nearby?
follow_ups.response: School, our yard, the soccer field, church, and sometimes grandparents' house.

follow_ups.question: What do you notice when you ride in the car around town?
follow_ups.response: Fields, barns, the school, and places where I imagine secret trails could be.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe when I am with my family or at school. I am not allowed to wander far by myself, especially near roads or fields.

follow_ups.question: What safety rules do your parents give you?
follow_ups.response: Stay where they can see me, do not go near the road, and tell them before I go to a friend's yard.

follow_ups.question: Is there any place that makes you nervous?
follow_ups.response: Dark places outside make me nervous, and big barking dogs if I do not know them.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is there is space to play and people know each other. The bad part is fun places like Disneyland are really far away, and sometimes there is not much to do if the weather is bad.

follow_ups.question: What do you do on bad-weather days?
follow_ups.response: I draw, build LEGO, read, or watch Frozen or Toy Story if my parents say okay.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite local event?
follow_ups.response: The county fair, because there are animals, rides, food, and lots of people I know.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live with my mom Sarah, my dad Mark, my brother Tyler, and our dog Daisy. My mom gets us ready for school and does lots of grown-up organizing. My dad works and fixes things around the house. Tyler is in preschool and likes cars, dinosaurs, and copying me. Nobody else is staying with us right now.

follow_ups.question: Who usually wakes up first?
follow_ups.response: My mom wakes up first, then she wakes me and Tyler. Dad is sometimes already getting ready.

follow_ups.question: Who shares a room?
follow_ups.response: I have my own room, and Tyler has his own room.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. Nobody is just staying for a little while.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone stayed temporarily before?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes cousins sleep over, but they do not live with us.

follow_ups.question: Does Daisy count to you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Daisy is permanent too.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my cousins stay overnight, or Grandma visits for dinner, but not all the time.

follow_ups.question: How often do cousins sleep over?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year, like summer or after family birthdays.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep?
follow_ups.response: Usually on an air mattress or in my room if it is my girl cousin.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. Everyone who lives here is home most nights.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone travel for work?
follow_ups.response: Not for a long time. Dad might be gone during the day, but he comes home.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone been away recently?
follow_ups.response: No, not like that.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: On school days I wake up around 7, get dressed, eat cereal or toast, and go to school. At school we do reading, math, recess, lunch, science or art, and sometimes music. After school I might have soccer, keyboard practice, homework, or just outside play. Wednesdays can have church activities sometimes, and weekends are different because we might visit grandparents, go to the store, do chores, or take a little road trip. Sunday usually feels calmer, with church and family time.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite part of a school day?
follow_ups.response: Recess and art, but also reading if the book has adventure or magic.

follow_ups.question: What time do you go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 8:30 on school nights, unless I keep asking for one more page.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not have a job because I am a kid. My work is going to school, doing homework, practicing keyboard, and helping a little at home. I have chores like putting clothes in the hamper, feeding Daisy with help, and cleaning up LEGO before someone steps on it. Sometimes school feels like a job because you have to sit still and finish worksheets. But I do not get paid like a grown-up.

follow_ups.question: What chore do you like best?
follow_ups.response: Feeding Daisy, because she gets excited and wags her tail.

follow_ups.question: What chore do you dislike?
follow_ups.response: Cleaning my room, because I find a toy and then I want to play instead.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I have to keep track of my backpack, library book, and school folder, but sometimes I misplace them. I brush my teeth morning and night, and I am supposed to read before bed. On soccer days I need my water bottle and shin guards. I also help Tyler sometimes, like getting him a crayon or telling him not to knock down my tower.

follow_ups.question: What do you misplace most often?
follow_ups.response: My pencil pouch or one shoe. Sometimes my folder is under drawings.

follow_ups.question: Who reminds you?
follow_ups.response: My mom mostly, and sometimes my teacher.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Soccer season changed things because some afternoons are busier now. I also have more reading homework than when I was little, and I can read chapter books by myself more. The weather getting warmer changed things because I can play outside longer after dinner. Sometimes we have school assembly practice, and then I think about my part all day.

follow_ups.question: How do busy afternoons feel?
follow_ups.response: Fun but rushy. We have to find my soccer stuff fast and eat a snack in the car.

follow_ups.question: What changed as you got better at reading?
follow_ups.response: I can stay up in my own story world longer without asking what every word means.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. I am the child. My weekday is school, recess, lunch, and then after school I might do soccer, keyboard, homework, drawing, or playing outside. Tyler goes to preschool and then plays at home.

follow_ups.question: What after-school activity matters most to you?
follow_ups.response: Soccer right now, because I like running with the team.

follow_ups.question: What do you do right after getting home?
follow_ups.response: I put my backpack down, have a snack, and sometimes forget to put the folder on the counter.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had a big experience with police. I have seen police cars at school safety things or at events, and they seemed nice. One time an officer talked about crossing streets and wearing seat belts. I know police are people you can ask for help if you are lost, but I also know grown-ups talk about serious things with police that I do not fully understand.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever spoken directly with an officer?
follow_ups.response: Only saying hi at a school or community event.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from the school safety talk?
follow_ups.response: Look both ways, buckle up, and do not run into the street after a ball.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing them at parades, school, or when a car has lights on by the road. I have not been in trouble with police.

follow_ups.question: How do flashing lights make you feel?
follow_ups.response: Curious and a little worried, because I wonder if someone got hurt.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents talk to you about police?
follow_ups.response: They say police can help in emergencies and that I should listen to safe grown-ups.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not know anyone close to me who has been arrested. Nobody in my family has told me about that.

follow_ups.question: Has that ever come up at school?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. We talk more about rules and safety.

follow_ups.question: Would you know who to ask if you were scared?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my parents or teacher.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I do not vote because I am eight. I know grown-ups vote for presidents and other leaders. Sometimes my parents talk about voting, but not in a way where I understand everything. At school we have voted for silly things before, like a favorite book or class reward, and I like that because everyone gets one choice.

follow_ups.question: What did you vote for in class?
follow_ups.response: I voted for extra art time once, but I think pajama day won.

follow_ups.question: Do you go with your parents when they vote?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I have gone along, but I mostly just stand there and wait.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I do not really have political views like grown-ups. I think people should be kind, share, follow fair rules, and help kids and animals. I care about things I understand, like playgrounds being safe, teachers having enough supplies, and people not being mean because someone is different. If I was making rules, I would want everyone to have food, a home, books, and doctors when they are sick. My parents sometimes have opinions about grown-up things, but I mostly think about whether something feels fair. I am still learning what Democrat and Republican mean.

follow_ups.question: Where do you learn about fairness?
follow_ups.response: At home, school, church, and also when kids argue at recess and the teacher helps us take turns.

follow_ups.question: What rule would you make at school?
follow_ups.response: Everybody should include someone who is left out at recess, and art supplies should not run out of pink or blue.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have not had a real change because I am still just learning. I know more words now than when I was little, like election and mayor and president. I used to think rules just appeared, but now I know people make them and argue about them. My ideas are still mostly about being fair and helping people.

follow_ups.question: What made you notice rules are made by people?
follow_ups.response: School, because our class helps choose some classroom rules, and because grown-ups talk about voting.

follow_ups.question: Do you like talking about politics?
follow_ups.response: Not really unless it is about something I understand, like school or animals.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have heard the words Black Lives Matter, but I do not know all the grown-up details. At school we learn that people have different skin colors and backgrounds and everyone should be treated kindly. It affects me mostly by making me think it is wrong to be mean or unfair to someone because of how they look. I have not gone to protests or anything like that.

follow_ups.question: Where did you first hear those words?
follow_ups.response: Probably from grown-ups talking or something on TV, but I do not remember exactly.

follow_ups.question: How do teachers explain fairness around race?
follow_ups.response: They say people should be respected and we read stories with different kinds of families and kids.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think it means people want others to listen when something is unfair or hurtful. I do not know how to fix big problems, but I know in my class it is bad to leave someone out or call them names. If someone says they are sad or scared, I think grown-ups should listen. That is how I understand it as a kid.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked about this with friends?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. We mostly talk about games, books, and soccer.

follow_ups.question: What do you do if someone is left out?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I ask if they want to play, especially if we need another person for tag.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I know I am white and I live in Iowa, and most people around me look kind of like me, but not everybody. I think people can have different skin, languages, foods, and holidays, and that can be interesting. I do not understand all of U.S. history yet, but I know some people were treated unfairly. My main thought is that everyone should be safe and included.

follow_ups.question: Have books or school lessons shaped this?
follow_ups.response: Yes, when we read books about different people and when teachers explain history in kid words.

follow_ups.question: Do you ask questions about differences?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but my mom says to ask respectfully and not make someone feel strange.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly keep my thoughts small and ask questions if I am confused. I have not joined protests. I try to be kind at school.

follow_ups.question: Who would you ask first?
follow_ups.response: My mom or my teacher.

follow_ups.question: What does being kind look like at school?
follow_ups.response: Letting people play, not laughing at mistakes, and saying sorry.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My parents sometimes talk about news, but they do not talk about it with me for a long time. They usually tell me everyone deserves respect and that serious problems need grown-ups to listen. At school, teachers talk about kindness more than politics. My friends do not really talk about it much.

follow_ups.question: Do adults disagree around you?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes grown-ups disagree about news, but I am usually sent to play or I stop listening.

follow_ups.question: What message do you remember most?
follow_ups.response: Treat people how you want to be treated.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I am pretty healthy. I run a lot, play soccer, climb trees, and have energy unless I stay up too late. I get colds sometimes, and I have had scraped knees and bruises from playing. I go to the doctor for checkups and shots. I do not have a big sickness that I know about.

follow_ups.question: What helps you feel strong?
follow_ups.response: Running, eating breakfast, drinking water, and sleeping enough.

follow_ups.question: What injuries happen most?
follow_ups.response: Scraped knees, bumps, and sometimes my legs get tired after soccer.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy because I like running and playing outside. It is hard when I want candy or when I do not want to stop reading and go to sleep. Vegetables are easier if they are on pizza or colorful. Winter makes it harder because I am inside more.

follow_ups.question: What healthy food do you like?
follow_ups.response: Strawberry-banana smoothies and rainbow veggie pizza with pepperoni and pineapple.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest at bedtime?
follow_ups.response: Stopping a story when I want to know what happens next.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing really big. I had colds and maybe a stomach bug, and I scraped myself playing outside. I have not broken a bone. I did have one time when I fell off a low tree branch and cried, but I was okay after ice and a bandage.

follow_ups.question: Did you go to the doctor for the fall?
follow_ups.response: No, my parents checked me and I was okay.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any chronic condition?
follow_ups.response: No, not that I know.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: If I am sick, I might miss school or soccer, and that is sad. But I do not have health problems that stop me most days.

follow_ups.question: What happens when you miss school?
follow_ups.response: I rest at home, and then I have to catch up on worksheets.

follow_ups.question: What do you miss most when sick?
follow_ups.response: Recess and seeing my friends.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Sometimes my brother gets sick from preschool germs, and then everyone has to wash hands a lot. My grandparents have grown-up aches sometimes, but I do not know all their medical stuff. If Mom or Dad is sick, the house feels different because they are tired. Nothing very scary has happened recently that I know about.

follow_ups.question: How do you help when someone is sick?
follow_ups.response: I try to be quieter, bring a blanket, or draw a get-well picture.

follow_ups.question: Does illness change your routine?
follow_ups.response: Yes, plans can get canceled, and we watch more quiet shows.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: My parents take care of appointments. We go to the doctor and dentist when we need to, and I have not been told we had to skip care. Sometimes I do not like waiting rooms or shots. We usually drive to where the appointment is, and Mom reminds me it will be quick.

follow_ups.question: What kind of care do you remember most?
follow_ups.response: Checkups, dentist cleanings, and shots.

follow_ups.question: What makes appointments easier?
follow_ups.response: A book, a sticker after, and knowing my mom is there.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really alternative medicine. At home we use normal things like soup, rest, honey for a cough if Mom says, and maybe a warm bath. We pray at church and at home sometimes, but if someone is really sick, we go to the doctor.

follow_ups.question: What home remedy do you like?
follow_ups.response: Soup and a blanket. Honey tastes better than some medicine.

follow_ups.question: Does prayer matter when someone is sick?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we might pray for them to feel better.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, I do not smoke or drink alcohol. I am a kid. If I am upset, I cry, draw, hug my mom, build LEGO, or go outside and run.

follow_ups.question: What helps fastest when you are upset?
follow_ups.response: A hug or drawing what happened.

follow_ups.question: Do adults around you smoke or drink?
follow_ups.response: Not around me much. I do not really pay attention to grown-up drinks.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or grown-up medicines. If I am sick, my parents give me kid medicine like fever medicine only when I need it. The most recent was probably cough or cold medicine, but I do not remember exactly. I do not take daily medicine.

follow_ups.question: Who decides when you take medicine?
follow_ups.response: My mom or dad.

follow_ups.question: Do you like taking medicine?
follow_ups.response: No, unless it tastes like grape, and even then not much.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: My parents handle paying and insurance. I know we have cards they bring to the doctor, but I do not understand the money part. For coping, we do regular checkups, wash hands, rest when sick, and try to eat decent food. I just follow what my parents say.

follow_ups.question: Do health costs get discussed with you?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. That is grown-up stuff.

follow_ups.question: What health rule do you hear most?
follow_ups.response: Wash your hands and brush your teeth.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I do not like shots because they pinch, but I get vaccines when my parents and doctor say I need them. I like the sticker after better than the shot.

follow_ups.question: Are you scared before shots?
follow_ups.response: A little. I try to look away.

follow_ups.question: Why do you get them anyway?
follow_ups.response: Because grown-ups say they help keep me from getting really sick.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my mom, dad, doctor, and school nurse. I do not look up vaccine information myself. If I have a question, I ask a grown-up I know. I also trust my teacher if she is explaining health rules at school.

follow_ups.question: Do you use the internet for health questions?
follow_ups.response: No, not by myself.

follow_ups.question: What question would you ask?
follow_ups.response: I would ask if it will hurt and how long it takes.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly happy and excited. I like school, soccer, drawing, and seeing my friends. Sometimes I get frustrated if Tyler messes with my things or if my LEGO build breaks. I also get nervous before performances or when I have to read out loud, but after I start it feels better. I feel proud when teachers like my stories or when I learn a new keyboard song.

follow_ups.question: What makes you happiest lately?
follow_ups.response: Soccer, finishing a drawing, and when my friends laugh at a story I made up.

follow_ups.question: What makes you worry?
follow_ups.response: Being late, forgetting something for school, or making a mistake in front of people.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: One time I had to do something in a school assembly, and I got scared I would forget my line. That morning my stomach felt twisty, and I told my mom I did not want to go. She helped me practice in the kitchen, and my teacher smiled at me before my turn. I said my line quietly but I did it. Afterward I felt like my whole body stopped being tight.

follow_ups.question: What did you do right after the assembly?
follow_ups.response: I found Emma and we talked about how scary the stage lights felt.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you feel about performing?
follow_ups.response: A little. I still get nervous, but now I know I can do it.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value my family, my friends, being kind, and having imagination. I like when people listen to each other and include each other. I value animals and nature too, because being outside makes me feel free. I also value making things, like stories, drawings, songs, and LEGO worlds, because then the ideas in my head become real.

follow_ups.question: What value do you try to practice every day?
follow_ups.response: Kindness, even though sometimes I get mad at Tyler.

follow_ups.question: What object feels special to you?
follow_ups.response: My LEGO pieces, my sketchbook, and my glittery stickers.

She has child-level savings behavior through a piggy bank, balancing desire for LEGO and art supplies with parental lessons to save and wait (Q61-Q64, Q83). Her time preferences are present-oriented but teachable: she wants toys and treats, yet can delay purchases by using wish lists or saving coins (Q60-Q62). She responds strongly to praise, inclusion, and visible progress in school, sports, keyboard, and art (Q01, Q43-Q44).

Her civic orientation is moral and relational rather than ideological: fairness, kindness, inclusion, safe schools, and helping people and animals are her dominant public values (Q24-Q30). summaries.psychologist: Melissa presents as imaginative, energetic, socially engaged, and curious, with a strong creative self-concept built around stories, LEGO worlds, drawing, music, and pretend play (Q01, Q07, Q109). She experiences age-appropriate nervousness before performances and new activities, but copes through practice, reassurance, drawing, parental support, and teacher encouragement (Q02, Q43-Q45, Q50). Her relational style is affiliative and collaborative, especially with friends and family, though she shows normal sibling frustration with her younger brother (Q05-Q07, Q45). Her motivational architecture blends mastery, praise, imagination, movement, and care for animals and nature, visible in her hopes to become an astronaut, artist, or veterinarian (Q108-Q109).
